issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Kiet Truong, a 44-year-old nurse of South Eastern Asian descent, still recalls the night he was mugged on his way home from a late shift at the hospital. It was a chilly autumn evening, and the dimly lit alleyway behind the building seemed like a shortcut to save time. As he walked, lost in thought about an upcoming patient's surgery, two men emerged from the shadows, their faces obscured by hoods. The next few minutes were a blur of chaos - Kiet remembers trying to shield his face as one attacker punched him while the other rummaged through his pockets. The pain in his jaw and temple still lingers in vivid detail, as if his body is replaying the assault with every flashback. The days that followed were marked by an increasing sense of hypervigilance. Kiet found himself constantly scanning the environment for potential threats - a habit he justified to himself as a necessary precaution in his line of work. On the job, he would meticulously check patients' rooms and corridors for any signs of danger, much to the confusion of his colleagues. At home, he would position himself near exits and scrutinize every stranger who walked by his house, convinced that the muggers might return. His wife, Linh, began to notice a change in him - how he'd jump at every creak of the floorboard or insist on sitting with his back against the wall at restaurants. As Kiet's anxiety intensified, so did his reliance on mental distractions. He would keep his mind occupied by mentally rehearsing patient care scenarios, analyzing medical charts, or replaying conversations from the day - anything to stave off the haunting memories of that night. Even in quiet moments, like during meditation or reading before bed, Kiet's thoughts would drift back to the mugging, and he'd relive the physical pain and fear all over again. Sleep became a luxury Kiet could no longer afford. He would lie awake for hours, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios - of being attacked again, of failing to protect himself or others. When he did manage to drift off, it was only to be jolted awake by the sound of footsteps outside or the rustling of leaves. His body seemed to have internalized the trauma, responding to every minor stimulus as if it were a life-or-death threat. One day, while on his rounds at the hospital, Kiet caught himself frantically searching for an escape route from a patient's room - a stark realization that his hypervigilance had started to compromise his work. That was when he knew he needed help. The weight of his memories, coupled with the crushing sense that nothing good could ever happen to him again, had become too much to bear. Kiet feared that if he couldn't shake off this all-consuming anxiety, it would ultimately destroy not just his career but also his relationships and his very sense of self. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with the sleeve of his jacket - a habitual gesture he'd developed since the mugging - Kiet revealed the despair that had taken hold: "I feel like I'm stuck in this nightmare, reliving it over and over, with no way out." His eyes pleaded for reassurance that there was still hope, that somehow, someway, he could rediscover a future worth living.
